summary: Describes an Extensible Authentication Protocol method for one-time password tokens, with particular advantages for tokens that connect electronically to their client. It supports one-way or mutual authentication and key material generation.

eli5.summary: Some keychain gadgets show a new code each time. EAP-POTP lets such a gadget prove who you are to a network and also helps make a secret key. This memo is informational.

questions: how do one-time password tokens work with eap
what is protected mode in eap-potp
how does eap-potp enable session resumption
subtitle: An authentication method for one-time password tokens over networks.

tldr.problem: One-time password tokens need a standard way to authenticate users in network protocols like PPP and 802.1X, with support for mutual authentication and key generation.
tldr.mechanism: EAP-POTP (EAP Protected One-Time Password) is an Extensible Authentication Protocol method that uses OTP tokens to prove a user's identity, optionally provides mutual authentication between client and server, and generates session keys.
tldr.outcome: Networks can authenticate users securely using handheld OTP tokens or tokens connected electronically to computers, with support for efficient session resumption and forward secrecy.

today: RFC 4793 is an Informational RFC that describes EAP-POTP, a framework for authenticating users with one-time password tokens over network protocols. It remains the standard reference for this protocol and has not been obsoleted.

sections.title: One-Time Password Tokens and Network Authentication
sections.content:
One-Time Password (OTP) tokens are small devices or software programs that generate codes usable only once, typically changing every 30 to 60 seconds. They provide strong user authentication without the weaknesses of fixed passwords. RFC 4793 describes EAP-POTP, an Extensible Authentication Protocol method designed to work with OTP tokens in network authentication scenarios.

EAP-POTP supports both simple unilateral authentication (where only the user proves their identity) and advanced mutual authentication (where the network also proves its identity to the user). It can generate session keys for protecting subsequent communications, and it includes a session resumption feature for devices that frequently reconnect to the same network, such as mobile devices switching between base stations. EAP-POTP is designed to work with any OTP algorithm but provides a specific profile for RSA SecurID tokens.
sections.eli5: Your keychain device shows a changing code. EAP-POTP lets your computer use that code to log into a network. The network can check the code, and if you want, it can also prove to you that it is the real network, not a fake one trying to trick you.

sections.title: How Authentication Works
sections.content:
EAP-POTP authentication involves three entities: the client (the user's computer with the EAP peer), the authenticator (the network access device), and a backend authentication server. The client obtains a one-time password from its OTP token, which is based on a shared secret seed stored on both the token and the authentication server. In unilateral mode, the client sends the OTP to prove knowledge of the seed; the server verifies it matches what it expects for that token.

In protected mode, which provides mutual authentication and integrity protection, the protocol is more sophisticated. The server sends a challenge, and the client combines the OTP with the challenge using a key derivation function (PBKDF2) to produce a Message Authentication Code (MAC). The server verifies this MAC and then sends its own MAC back to the client, proving it knows the shared secret. Only after mutual authentication succeeds do both parties derive keying material (a Master Session Key and Extended Master Session Key) for protecting the rest of the session.
sections.eli5: The network asks for a code from your token. You send it. In basic mode, that is enough. In protected mode, the network also sends you a proof that it knows the secret, and you exchange codes that prove you both have the same secret seed.

sections.title: Design and Protocol Exchange
sections.content:
EAP-POTP uses a TLV (Type-Length-Value) format for its messages, making messages easy for software to parse without user interaction. The protocol begins with version negotiation: the server sends its supported version range, and the client responds with the highest version it supports within that range. If versions do not overlap, authentication fails and another method must be tried. This design allows for future protocol improvements while maintaining backward compatibility with older implementations.

The protocol flow involves multiple exchanges. The server sends an initial request with an OTP TLV, optional server information (including a session identifier), and cryptographic algorithm preferences. The client generates an OTP using its token, optionally encrypts it with derived keys (protected mode), and returns it. The server verifies the OTP and, if authentication is successful and protected mode is used, sends a Confirm TLV. The client verifies this confirmation, confirming the server's identity, and both parties now share validated session keys. Optionally, the server can request a new PIN or other additional operations before sending a success indication.
sections.eli5: First, the computer and network agree on what version of the protocol to use. Then the network asks for a code. The computer gets it from the token and sends it. In protected mode, they swap proof messages to make sure both are real. Finally, the network says okay, and both have secret keys they share.

sections.title: Key Derivation and Session Security
sections.content:
EAP-POTP uses PBKDF2 (a password-based key derivation function) to convert the OTP and other inputs into cryptographic keys. The default PRF (pseudo-random function) for PBKDF2 is HMAC-SHA256. The output includes five keys: K_MAC for message authentication, K_ENC for encrypting sensitive data, SRK for session resumption, and the standard EAP Master Session Key (MSK) and Extended Master Session Key (EMSK) for use by other protocols. The MSK is 64 octets and the EMSK is 64 octets, conforming to EAP standards.

To defend against brute-force attacks on short OTPs, EAP-POTP supports a pepper mechanism: a secret value unknown to attackers that is combined with the OTP in key derivation. The pepper can be generated by the client or provided by the server in protected form. Session resumption allows a client to reconnect to the same server without re-entering an OTP; instead, it sends a digest of the previous session keys, reducing authentication latency for mobile devices.
sections.eli5: The OTP is mixed with other secrets using special math to make strong keys that lock down the conversation. Some keys protect messages, others help you log in faster next time. To stop hackers trying every possible code, there is an extra secret number (pepper) that only you and the network know.

sections.title: Security and Attack Protection
sections.content:
EAP-POTP addresses several security threats. Man-in-the-middle attacks are prevented by mutual authentication in protected mode: both client and server prove knowledge of the shared secret. Eavesdropping is mitigated by encrypting sensitive data with K_ENC when in protected mode. The use of PBKDF2 with a high iteration count slows brute-force attacks on the OTP. Replay attacks are prevented by the use of challenges and the MAC calculations based on the message sequence; an attacker cannot reuse a previous authentication exchange.

One threat specific to OTP systems is the race attack: an attacker intercepts an OTP just as the user generates it and races the legitimate user to submit it to the authentication server first. EAP-POTP does not fully prevent this (no protocol can without out-of-band communication), but the use of per-message MACs and sequence-dependent hashing makes exploitation harder. The protocol also allows servers to request new PINs if a PIN is suspected to be compromised, and it supports the use of a pepper for additional entropy.
sections.eli5: The network checks that the computer is real by asking it to prove it knows the secret. The computer checks that the network is real the same way. If someone listens to your conversation, they only hear scrambled keys and codes, not your passwords. The protocol keeps track of every message so old ones cannot be replayed.

sections.title: Integration with EAP Protocols
sections.content:
EAP-POTP is designed to work within protocols that support the Extensible Authentication Protocol, including PPP (Point-to-Point Protocol), IEEE 802.1X (network port access control), and IKEv2 (Internet Key Exchange). When used within 802.1X, EAP-POTP can control access to wired and wireless networks. In IKEv2, it can provide authentication and key material for VPN tunnels. The RFC includes profiles for specific OTP algorithms, starting with RSA SecurID.

The document also specifies how the generated MSK and EMSK are used with RADIUS attributes such as MPPE (Microsoft Point-to-Point Encryption) keys, allowing the authentication server to configure encryption for PPP sessions. Appendix B provides detailed examples of authentication exchanges for various scenarios: basic unilateral authentication, mutual authentication, session resumption, and PIN updates.
sections.eli5: EAP-POTP works with Wi-Fi login, VPN software, and dial-up connections. Wherever a network needs to check who you are using a code-generating device, EAP-POTP can be used. It hands the network the keys it needs to scramble your connection afterward.
